claims.text: High-temperature stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is primarily governed by intrinsic lattice distortion.
A random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii produces significant lattice distortion in the initial nanoparticles.
Adding a small concentration of an element with a distinct atomic radius will reduce the overall atomic-size mismatch and lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion manifests as local strain fields and atomic-level heterogeneity.
Lattice distortion elevates the activation energy for dislocation motion.
Lattice distortion elevates the activation energy for atomic diffusion.
A large lattice distortion increases the energy barrier for atomic rearrangements and thereby hinders diffusion.
Diffusion inhibition caused by lattice distortion suppresses phase segregation.
Diffusion inhibition caused by lattice distortion suppresses precipitate nucleation.
Baseline nanoparticles with high lattice distortion will undergo less phase separation than doped nanoparticles with reduced lattice distortion.
Baseline nanoparticles with high lattice distortion will form fewer precipitates than doped nanoparticles with reduced lattice distortion.
Baseline nanoparticles with high lattice distortion will retain better structural integrity than reduced-distortion doped nanoparticles.
Reducing lattice distortion will increase diffusion-driven degradation during accelerated aging.
Reducing lattice distortion will increase high-temperature phase transitions during accelerated aging.
The proposed lattice-distortion mechanism applies throughout 473–1923 K.
The proposed lattice-distortion mechanism applies to low noble-metal-content systems.
Severe oxidation or mechanical loading could independently affect nanoparticle stability.
Surface diffusion may compete with bulk lattice distortion in governing nanoscale stability.
Dopant-induced local compositional changes may independently influence stability.
